1121.title: A hymn in Kanara
1121.hook: Guru Arjan's hymn of a person with no enemy and no stranger, and how he got there
1121.howItsDone: Guru Arjan's Kanara hymn is sung in kirtan in gurdwaras and at home, in Raga Kanara.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Kanara, and your line was night: a mind turned green by good company. A new week starts now.

The person at the next table. The driver. A name scrolling past in the comments. Not disliked, exactly; just not counted yet. That's what a stranger is. A hymn of Guru Arjan in Raga Kanara says, in plain English: no one is my enemy, no one is a stranger. It's a big thing for anyone to say, and the second half asks more than the first. The hymn says that whole category has emptied out. And it tells you how.
screen: `NO ONE IS MY ENEMY.` → `NO ONE IS A STRANGER.` → `AND IT TELLS YOU HOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the hymn, in paraphrase, in its own order. It begins with what went missing: I have forgotten all my jealousy of others, ever since I found the company of the holy. Then the line we started with: no one is my enemy, no one is a stranger; I get along with everyone. Then: whatever God does, I accept as good; this wisdom I received from the holy. And it ends: the One God is present in all, and seeing this, Nanak blossoms. The order is building something. First, jealousy goes, the quiet engine behind a lot of distance between people: comparing, keeping score. With it gone, enemies are harder to keep. Then strangers go too, because the last line explains why nobody is foreign anymore: the same One is present in every one of them. And the source of all of it is named twice: the company of the holy. That's yesterday's thread, picked up in the same raga. Guru Ram Das's mind turned green in good company; in Guru Arjan's hymn, that same company empties out jealousy, enemies and strangers. The word for stranger here is bigana, an outsider, someone who isn't one of yours. The hymn doesn't say strangers stop existing. It says that from where this person stands, there aren't any left. And the closing image isn't a rule but a flowering: seeing the One in everyone, Nanak blossoms. Your line: no stranger.
screen: `FIRST, JEALOUSY IS FORGOTTEN.` · `NO ENEMY, NO STRANGER.` · `WHATEVER GOD DOES, ACCEPTED AS GOOD.` · `THE ONE IN ALL; NANAK BLOSSOMS.` · then, large: `NO STRANGER.`

segments.voice: If you can, play this hymn or another shabad sung in Kanara, or sit in the quiet, and bring to mind someone you passed today without really seeing: a cashier, a neighbor, a face on a screen. Let them stand in front of you for a few breaths, with a morning, a family and a worry of their own, and let them stop being background. If you pray, hold the hymn's last thought, that the One is present in them too; if you don't, simply let them count.
A hymn in Kanara. Guru Arjan's song of forgetting jealousy in the company of the holy, until no one is an enemy, no one a stranger, and the One is seen in all. Today's word.
Your line: no stranger. In Guru Arjan's hymn, it all starts with forgetting jealousy. See you tomorrow.

1122.title: Raga Kalyan
1122.hook: the dishes are done, the lights come on, and the Granth turns to an evening raga that opens with a child and a parent
1122.howItsDone: In kirtan, shabads from the Kalyan section, by Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan, are sung in Raga Kalyan, which tradition associates with the evening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Kanara, and your line was no stranger: Guru Arjan's song of no enemy and no stranger. Today the Granth turns to evening.

The last plate goes in the rack. Somebody switches on a lamp. Outside, the streetlights are on. The day's noise has moved off into the next street: a kettle, a television low in another room, a child being called in. The Guru Granth Sahib has a raga that tradition sings in this hour, as night begins. Its name is Kalyan, and it opens with a family picture.
screen: `THE LAST PLATE IN THE RACK.` → `THE LAMPS COME ON.` → `A RAGA FOR THIS HOUR.`

segments.voice: In the Granth's order, Kalyan comes right after Kanara, and its pages hold hymns of Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan. Tradition places it in the first part of the night and calls its mood calm and settled. Teachers of raga describe moods in different ways, so hold that as tradition, not as a rule written in the Granth. What is written is the opening hymn, by Guru Ram Das. In paraphrase: no one has found the limit of the Lord who is in everything. We are your children; you are the one who looks after us. You are the great Being, my father and my mother. Notice the move. The first line goes as big as it can: no limit, no end anyone has reached. The very next breath comes all the way home. Children. A father. A mother. The infinite and the kitchen table, side by side. Evening is the hour when children are called in, when whoever looks after a house counts heads and closes the door. The hymn hangs the whole of creation on that ordinary scene. Whatever the day was, the one who sustains it is described as a parent. Peace, in this opening, isn't silence or emptiness. It's the feeling of a child who knows someone is watching the door. Sikhs who sing Kalyan in the evening sing it into exactly the hour when that picture is easiest to see.
screen: `AFTER KANARA: GURU RAM DAS, GURU ARJAN.` · `TRADITION: AN EVENING RAGA.` · `NO ONE HAS FOUND THE LIMIT.` · `WE ARE YOUR CHILDREN.` · then, large: `PEACEFUL EVENING.`

segments.voice: If you can, play a shabad sung in Raga Kalyan; it doesn't need to be evening where you are, and if you can't, simply sit in the quiet. Then call the day's pieces in one by one, the way someone calls children in from the street, the meeting, the errand, the thing you said too fast, and let the door close behind each. If you pray, rest in Guru Ram Das's picture of the One who looks after us like a father and a mother; if you don't, let the house of your mind go quiet.
Raga Kalyan. The raga that follows Kanara, which tradition sings as night begins, opening with Guru Ram Das's hymn: no one has found your limit, and we are your children. Today's word.
Your line: peaceful evening. The one who sustains the day is pictured as a parent at the door. Until tomorrow.

1123.title: Listening in Kalyan
1123.hook: a bee that keeps coming back, a bird that waits for one drop: reading along with a short hymn of Guru Arjan in Kalyan
1123.howItsDone: Sikhs often read a shabad with a translation open while it is sung in kirtan; some gurdwaras project the Gurmukhi and an English rendering on a screen so the congregation can follow line by line.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Kalyan, and your line was peaceful evening: a hymn that calls the limitless One father and mother.

A bumblebee on a lavender bush doesn't land once and leave. It circles, and comes back to the same flower, again and again. Nobody has to persuade it; something there is sweet enough. Kalyan, the evening raga, holds hymns of Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan, and one of Guru Arjan's is built around that bee. It's short enough to read from start to finish, so today it gets read slowly, line by line.
screen: `A BEE THAT KEEPS COMING BACK.` → `TWO GURUS IN KALYAN.` → `A HYMN SHORT ENOUGH TO READ ALONG.`

segments.voice: The hymn opens with its center line, the one marked Rahao, pause. In paraphrase: grant me this grace, that like the bee drawn to the nectar of the lotus, my mind is drawn to your lotus feet, again and again. In Gurmukhi, again and again is fer fer, and you can hear it turning back on itself. That's the whole prayer of the hymn: not one visit, but a mind that keeps returning. The first verse brings in a bird, the chatrik, the rainbird from Malar's rain pictures, which tradition says drinks only drops of rain. In paraphrase: I have no business with any other water; give this rainbird the drop of the Lord. The second verse closes it: without meeting, there is no contentment; seeing the vision, Nanak lives. Guru Arjan signs the hymn with the name Nanak. Now hear it with Kalyan's evening around it. The bee isn't calm because it stopped moving. It's calm because it knows where it's going back to. The rainbird isn't calm because it's full; it knows which drop it's waiting for. Contentment here, santokh, isn't having everything. It's being turned toward one thing. That's a peace an evening can hold: not an empty room, but a mind that has found its flower and keeps landing there. Read it once, and when you hear Kalyan sung, you'll know where the bee is.
screen: `RAHAO: DRAWN AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `THE RAINBIRD WANTS ONE DROP.` · `NO CONTENTMENT WITHOUT MEETING.` · `PEACE IS BEING TURNED TOWARD ONE THING.` · then, large: `EVENING PEACE.`

segments.voice: If you can, find this hymn of Guru Arjan in Kalyan with a translation beside it, and read it once, slowly, while it's sung or in silence. Then sit and choose one thing to return to: the breath at the nostrils or, if you pray, the word Waheguru. The mind will wander, and the bee wanders too; each time you notice, come back to the same place, gently, without counting and without scolding.

Your line: evening peace. It isn't having everything; it's being turned toward one thing. See you tomorrow.

1124.title: Raga Prabhati
1124.hook: the Granth turns from evening to daybreak, and Guru Nanak's first Prabhati hymn names what to put on before anything else
1124.howItsDone: Sikh practice treasures the early hours, amrit vela, for reciting Gurbani; in some gurdwaras the morning kirtan includes shabads sung in Raga Prabhati.

segments.voice: Yesterday, listening in Kalyan, and your line was evening peace: the bee that comes back to the lotus, again and again.

What's the first thing you put on in the morning? Glasses, maybe. A watch, a ring from the nightstand. A turban, tied fresh, fold by fold, before the house is awake. Whatever it is, it goes on before the day can ask anything of you. For two days the Granth has been in the evening. Now it turns a page and the sky is getting light. The raga is Prabhati, tradition sings it at dawn, and Guru Nanak opens it with something to wear.
screen: `WHAT GOES ON FIRST?` → `EVENING TURNS TO DAYBREAK.` → `A HYMN ABOUT WHAT TO WEAR.`

segments.voice: In the Granth's order, Prabhati follows Kalyan. Hymns of the Gurus open it, then come Bhagats whose words the Gurus set beside their own, Kabir among them. Tradition sings Prabhati at the edge of light; teachers describe raga moods differently, so take the timing as tradition, not as a rule in the text. The text is Guru Nanak's opening hymn. In paraphrase: by your Name we cross over. Your Name is honor, and it is worship. Your Name is my ornament, and the aim of my understanding. Without the Name, there is never honor. Then the Rahao: all other cleverness is only show; whoever you forgive, their work is made complete. An ornament is the thing you put on so it's seen, the finishing touch. Guru Nanak gives that word to the Name. So in the dawn raga, the first thing to put on isn't a watch or a ring. It's remembering. Sikhs call the hours before dawn amrit vela, the ambrosial time, and in the Japji, Guru Nanak links that hour with the true Name and reflection on greatness. Prabhati sings into the same hour. Hear the Rahao in the morning, too. Early is when the mind starts planning: what to say, how to win, how to look. The hymn doesn't throw planning away. It puts it second. First the Name, the ornament. Then the day.
screen: `PRABHATI FOLLOWS KALYAN.` · `TRADITION: SUNG AT DAYBREAK.` · `YOUR NAME IS MY ORNAMENT.` · `ALL OTHER CLEVERNESS IS SHOW.` · then, large: `DAWN.`

segments.voice: Sit as if it were early, the house quiet, the light thin, the breath slow and even, and if you can, play a shabad sung in Raga Prabhati. Before any plan for the day takes shape, let the first thing you put on be something other than a plan: if you pray, Waheguru, said once on the breath; if you don't, a minute of simple attention. When the clever thoughts arrive, let them wait at the door.
Raga Prabhati. The raga that follows Kalyan, which tradition sings at daybreak, opening with Guru Nanak's hymn: your Name is my ornament, and all other cleverness is only show. Today's word.
Your line: dawn. The Name goes on first, like an ornament, before any cleverness. Until tomorrow.

1125.title: A hymn in Prabhati
1125.hook: Kabir's hymn in Prabhati starts with one light and ends with a question: so who is good, and who is bad?
1125.howItsDone: Kabir's hymn of the one light is sung in kirtan in Raga Prabhati and is sometimes quoted when Sikhs speak of the equality of all people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Prabhati, and your line was dawn: Guru Nanak's Name worn as an ornament, before any cleverness.

So who is good, and who is bad? People ask it about strangers on the news, the neighbors, the driver who just cut in, usually with an answer already waiting. In the Prabhati section of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Bhagat Kabir asks it too, in a hymn the Gurus placed among their own. But he asks it at the end of a sentence that begins with light, and by the time the question arrives, a ready answer may not fit.
screen: `SO WHO IS GOOD, AND WHO IS BAD?` → `KABIR, IN PRABHATI.` → `A QUESTION THAT BEGINS WITH LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the opening, in paraphrase. First, God brought forth the light, and from that power came all people. From one light the whole world sprang up. So who is good, and who is bad? Kabir uses the name Allah here, and the word noor for light; in other hymns he calls the One Ram, among other names. Then the Rahao: people, don't wander lost in doubt. The Creator is in the creation, and the creation is in the Creator, filling every place. Then Kabir picks up a pot. The clay is one; the Maker shaped it in many ways. There's no fault in the clay pots, and no fault in the potter. The One is in everything, and all of it happens by the Maker's doing. Whoever recognizes the Maker's will, the hukam, knows the One. The hymn closes with Kabir himself: the Guru gave him something sweet, his fear went, and he sees the Pure One everywhere. Set that at daybreak, where tradition sings Prabhati. Dawn light doesn't pick. It reaches the dome of the gurdwara and the alley behind it, the person you love and the person you can't stand. If everyone is clay from one pit, shaped by one hand, lit by one light, then good and bad stop being two kinds of people. The hymn doesn't say no one does wrong. It says no one is made of different stuff.
screen: `FROM ONE LIGHT, THE WHOLE WORLD.` · `THE CREATOR IN THE CREATION.` · `ONE CLAY, MANY POTS.` · `DAWN LIGHT DOESN'T PICK.` · then, large: `LIGHT AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: If you can, play Kabir's hymn of the one light, or another shabad sung in Prabhati; if not, sit in the quiet. Let the breath go out toward one person you love, then one you hardly know, whoever delivered your last parcel, then, gently, someone you find hard, the same breath and the same light reaching all three, the way morning reaches every street. If you pray, remember the one light Kabir names; if you don't, simply notice the three faces side by side.

1126.title: Raga Jaijavanti
1126.hook: where the Granth's ragas end, one voice sings alone: Guru Tegh Bahadur, and a kingdom built like a wall of sand
1126.howItsDone: Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns in Raga Jaijavanti are sung in kirtan, and Sikh tradition remembers him as the Guru who gave his life for others' freedom of faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Prabhati, and your line was light at dawn: Kabir's one light, and one clay shaped into many pots.

A sandcastle at the edge of the tide can be a fine thing: towers, a moat, a wall patted smooth with both hands. Everyone on the beach knows how the story ends, and still somebody builds it. The Guru Granth Sahib's long run of ragas has gone from evening to dawn and back. Today it reaches the place where the ragas end, a section called Jaijavanti that holds a single voice, and in its first hymn, a wall made of sand.
screen: `A WALL PATTED SMOOTH WITH BOTH HANDS.` → `WHERE THE RAGAS END.` → `ONE VOICE, AND A WALL OF SAND.`

segments.voice: Jaijavanti follows Prabhati, and it is the last of the raga sections in the Granth's order. After it come verses gathered without a raga heading, and at the very end a page that comes up in two days. Jaijavanti is short, and every hymn in it is by Guru Tegh Bahadur. Tradition says his hymns were added to the Granth by his son, Guru Gobind Singh. In many ragas, voices take turns: Gurus, then Bhagats. Here one voice sings alone, the way a concert sometimes ends with a single singer. The first hymn opens with a doubled call, in paraphrase: remember the Lord, remember the Lord; this alone is your work. Leave clinging to Maya, the world's glitter, and take shelter with God. Count the world's pleasures as false; the whole show is false. Then two pictures. Wealth is like riches in a dream. And the rule of the whole earth is like a wall of sand. Hear how gently that's put. The hymn doesn't sneer at wealth or power. A dream can be vivid; a sand wall can be well made. The point is what they're made of, and how long they stand. Against that, one thing is named as your work: remembering. Remembering the One, twice over, so you hear it. After all the moods, morning and evening, spring and rain, the last raga sets down a plain instruction.

1127.title: A hymn in Jaijavanti
1127.hook: it's passing, it's passing: Guru Tegh Bahadur talks to the mind about time, and the week looks back
1127.howItsDone: Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns, including those in Jaijavanti, are sung in kirtan; his saloks near the end of the Granth are also read at the close of a full reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Jaijavanti, and your line was the last raga: Guru Tegh Bahadur sings alone, remember, remember, this is your work.

Departing. Departing. On a station board the word blinks beside a train that hasn't moved yet. The doors are still open. People are walking, not running. The word isn't a disaster; it's information, said twice so nobody misses it. Guru Tegh Bahadur has a hymn in Jaijavanti that opens the same way, with one word said twice: it's passing, it's passing. It's the last day of this week, so there's a look back over the ragas, too. But first, the board, and the doors still open.
screen: `DEPARTING. DEPARTING.` → `THE DOORS ARE STILL OPEN.` → `ONE WORD, SAID TWICE.`

segments.voice: The hymns in Jaijavanti keep speaking to the mind directly. One asks it: O mind, what will become of you? This one opens, in paraphrase: it is passing, it is passing, your life is passing to no purpose. Day and night you hear holy stories, and still you don't take them in, the same charge Parmanand made in Sarang. The time has come; where will you run? The body you counted on as steady will turn to dust. Why not remember the Name of the Lord? In Gurmukhi the opening is beet jaihai, beet jaihai, and the doubling does what the station board does. It isn't shouting. It's making sure. The hymn is blunt, even calling the mind a fool, but it isn't despair. It names time honestly, and in the same breath points to what can still be done: remember. The doors are open. Yesterday's hymn said remembering is your work; today's says the work has a clock. Now the week. Guru Arjan in Kanara: no enemy, no stranger. Kalyan in the evening: we are your children, and the bee that comes back again and again. Prabhati at dawn: the Name as the ornament you put on first, and Kabir's one light on every street. Jaijavanti, where the ragas end: remember, this is your work. And today, the reason to start now. Evening, dawn and the end of the ragas, with the same Name running through all of them.
screen: `O MIND, WHAT WILL BECOME OF YOU?` · `IT'S PASSING, IT'S PASSING.` · `NOT A THREAT: THE DOORS ARE OPEN.` · `THE WEEK: STRANGER, CHILD, LIGHT, SAND.` · then, large: `BEFORE IT SLIPS BY.`

segments.voice: If you can, play Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymn of beet jaihai, or another in Jaijavanti; if not, sit in the quiet and feel this breath come in and go out, passing, and the next one passing too. Don't hold on, and don't hurry: be present for each one before it goes, the way you'd step through open doors without running. If you pray, remember the Name on each breath, as the hymn asks; if you don't, let each breath be fully noticed before it slips by.
A hymn in Jaijavanti. Guru Tegh Bahadur's song to the mind: it's passing, it's passing; why not remember the Name while there's time? Today's word.
Your line: before it slips by. The board says departing, and the doors are still open. A week of ragas, done.
